newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania President denies bid to control banks.
newsitem.headline: Romania President denies bid to control banks.

text.p: Romania's President on Monday rejected allegations by the leftist opposition that the ruling coalition planned to bring state banks and utilities under political control and vowed to use his office to enforce laws.
"The President of Romania will use his authority as well as all his constitutional powers to ensure full observance of laws," Emil Constantinescu said in a statement printed in Bucharest dailies.

The statement was in response to attacks led by the Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), saying the centrist coalition planned to appoint party loyalists to key posts on the boards of state-run public utilities and commercial banks.

In a weekend statement, the PDSR cited the Banca Comerciala Romana SA, Banca Agricola, Banca Romana pentru Dezvoltare SA, Bancorex SA and Banc Post among the main banking institutions targeted by the coalition, which ousted the PDSR in last November's elections.

Any attempt to bring those banks under political control would have "destabilising and harmful" effects on the country's banking system, the PDSR said, adding that the authorities were acting in an authoritarian way.
"They are interested in acquiring all levers of economic activity, to control civic activity."
Constantinescu said the PDSR wanted to mislead the media.

"Such allegations could generate confusion and mistrust in the banking system and in the reform process. They could lead to political and social tensions liable to affect Romania's stability and its national security," Constantinescu said.

Privatisation of banks was a priority of the government headed by Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, Constantinescu said. The cabinet, he said, was expected this week to submit a bill on bank privatisation to parliament for approval .
"Under the present rules any changes on the banks' boards can be made only through a secret vote of the board, which in its turn is appointed by the shareholders' meeting...," Constantinescu said.

Romania's privatisation programme, launched in 1995 after long delays, has so far failed to deal with banks and large utilities, which form the core of the economy and offer the best hope of attracting big foreign investment.
